Hebrew often says X of Y by putting two nouns side by side. There is no word for of. This is called the construct state, or smichut. The first noun, the one that owns or describes, often shortens or changes its ending, and it can never take the word for the. Only the second noun can carry it, and then the whole chain counts as definite. A plural first noun often ends in an -ei sound instead of -im. So a tree of life is simply tree, life, and children of Israel is children, Israel. A dash called a maqaf sometimes ties the pair into a single written word. In the examples below, the chains come straight from prayer and Torah lines. The English meaning is written beside each one. For about forty years the Jewish families of Simcoe County met as the Simcoe County Jewish Association, gathering for holiday services and events in one another's homes and in rented premises. Members lived not only in Barrie but in Collingwood, Gravenhurst and other towns across the region. By 2000 the community had grown to about 100 families, had raised $100,000 of its own money toward a first synagogue, and drew 150 people to Yom Kippur services; that July it received a Torah scroll donated by B'nai Tikvah Congregation in Niagara Falls.

Rabbi Wittstein led the congregation until his death in January 2010 at the age of 74. Rabbi Michal Shekel of Toronto served as interim rabbi, and in June 2010 Rabbi Debra Stahlberg Dressler, newly ordained at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati after a first career in direct marketing and magazine circulation, became the congregation's second spiritual leader and London's first full-time female rabbi. She co-founded the London Interfaith Peace Camp, which brings Jewish, Christian and Muslim young people together, and serves as principal of the religious school.

Solel has grown to more than 300 member families and runs a religious and language school two days a week for preschoolers to adults. Since 1980 it has been twinned with Kehilat Darchei Noam in Ramat HaSharon, Israel, and it has led several missions there. The congregation celebrated its fiftieth anniversary in 2023-24, re-enacting the walk from the Glen Erin Inn to Folkway Drive.

text: For years the congregation made do with borrowed space, one year holding its High Holy Day services at a golf course. It later moved into a larger building in the heart of downtown Newmarket, near the public library, using two of the three floors for services, programming and its Hebrew school. Rabbi Jonathan Crane, who worked part-time with the congregation and led its High Holy Day services at the time, said the move gave Or Hadash a real footprint in Newmarket and in Ontario.

The congregation's first rabbi, serving on weekends, was Sherwin Wine, another Detroit assistant, who in 1963 would found the Birmingham Temple and with it Humanistic Judaism. A large house on Ouellette Avenue served as an early home. In 1961 the congregation accepted a gift of land and left the downtown; the cornerstone of the present synagogue on Mark Avenue was laid in July 1962, and an addition followed in 1981.

Holy Blossom Temple dates its history to September 1856, when Lewis Samuel, an immigrant from York, England, and seventeen Jewish families from Britain and Europe met to form a congregation and plan High Holy Day services; a Toronto Hebrew Congregation had already been holding services in homes since 1849 and had founded the Pape Avenue cemetery, Toronto's first Jewish burial ground, which passed to the new congregation in 1858. The Ontario Heritage Trust recognises Holy Blossom as the first Jewish congregation in Ontario, and in 2001 placed a plaque there.
